mcqs.question: The edge-update formula `new_sum = old_sum - arr[i-k] + arr[i]` relies on which property of the aggregate?
options: That the aggregate value is always positive
That removing an element's contribution can be undone by a single inverse operation, as subtraction does for a running sum
That the underlying array is sorted
That the window size k is an even number
mcqs.explanation: Sum works because subtracting an element's value exactly reverses having added it — that reversibility is what the formula depends on, not sign, sortedness, or parity of k, none of which the sliding-window mechanics care about.

mcqs.question: When a fixed-size window slides from indices [1,3] to [2,4], which values actually change the running sum?
options: All three values inside the new window get re-added to the running sum
Only the value entering at the new right edge changes the sum
The value entering at the new right edge and the value leaving at the old left edge — the shared middle elements stay untouched
The minimum and maximum values within the new window
mcqs.explanation: Two consecutive fixed-size windows share every element except the one that leaves and the one that enters, so only those two values need to touch the running aggregate — re-adding all three, or ignoring the outgoing value, would both produce a wrong sum.

mcqs.question: A sliding-window loop calls `sum(arr[i-k+1:i+1])` fresh on every iteration instead of doing the subtract-then-add update. What's actually wrong with this?
options: It raises an IndexError as soon as i approaches the end of the array
It produces a different, incorrect final answer compared to the O(1)-update version
It still produces the correct answer but silently reverts the algorithm back to O(n·k), erasing the sliding-window speedup
It only produces correct results when k happens to be odd
mcqs.explanation: Recomputing the slice sum every step gives the same correct answer as the O(1) update — the bug is purely a performance regression back to O(n·k), which is easy to miss because the output looks right on small test cases. It doesn't raise any exception and has nothing to do with the parity of k.

mcqs.question: What actually happens if k is larger than the array's length and the code has no explicit guard for it?
options: Python raises an IndexError immediately when building the first window
The first window's sum silently computes over fewer than k elements, corrupting every subsequent edge-update since the math assumes a full window of exactly k
The function automatically returns None without needing any special-case code
The code still works correctly, just with an effectively shorter window size
mcqs.explanation: Python slicing beyond the array's bounds doesn't error — it just returns whatever elements exist, so the 'first window' quietly has fewer than k elements, and every later subtract-then-add step assumes a full window that was never actually there. Nothing raises automatically, and the result is wrong, not merely a shorter but valid window.

mcqs.question: Why can't Sliding Window Maximum use the same subtract-then-add trick as Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K?
options: Because arrays used for max-tracking must always be sorted before applying the window
Because Sliding Window Maximum doesn't actually use a fixed-width window
Because computing a maximum is inherently slower than computing a sum regardless of technique
Max and min can't be undone by a single inverse operation — the outgoing element might have been the window's max, and a running scalar doesn't track the next-largest remaining value
mcqs.explanation: Sum is reversible by subtraction, but there's no equivalent inverse for max — once the current max leaves the window, recovering the new max requires knowing every remaining value's relative order, which a single running number can't capture. Sliding Window Maximum does use a fixed width; the issue is entirely about the aggregate, not the window itself, and no sorting requirement is involved.
